background.definition: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) is defined as pain localized to the lower back that persists for more than 3 months.

list.listitem: Prevalence: 40.9% of all adults, based on 2019 US National Health Interview Survey. The prevalence may be much higher in people of color in underserved areas. It is the second most prevalent type of chronic pain in the US, after chronic pain from composite of hip, knees, and feet.

Data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2009 to 2010 reported that the prevalence of CLBP in US adults ages 20 to 69 years was 13.1%. It increases with age with the highest likelihood in the 5th and 6th decade of life, is higher in women, and white people are 1.5 times more likely to report having chronic LBP than African Americans or Hispanics.

According to the 2019 US National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (NAMCS), back pain is the 13th most common reason for visit accounting for 3.5% of all office-based visits in the US. Median age was 55 years, 58.2% were female, and imaging studies (eg, X-ray, MRI) were ordered in 21.6% of visits.
According to the 2020 NAMCS for Community Health Centers, back pain is the 10th most common reason for visits.

Prevalence: Across the globe, at any moment an estimated 7% of people have LBP. Lifetime prevalence is estimated at 38%. People 40 to 69 years old and those with socio-economic hardships are more likely to experience LBP. In adults 60 years and older, prevalence of CLBP is 36% according to a meta-analysis involving different countries.

In 2016, back pain was the 9th most common reason for visit reported by clinicians, but the 2nd most common reason for visit reported by patients. Additionally, back pain was the 4th most common reason for a medical visit in developed countries, but was not among the top 10 reasons for a visit in developing countries.

In 2013, low back pain accounted for the third highest amount of health care spending in the US amounting to 87.6 billion USD. By 2016, it had moved up (along with neck pain) to being the highest cost of health care spending estimated at about 134.5 billion USD.
CLBP leads to higher healthcare utilization, lower health-related quality of life and worse health outcomes (both physical and mental) particularly in people of color in underserved areas.
In the US, LBP was the third leading cause of disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) from 1990 to 2016.
In the UK in 2013, people with CLBP incurred double the healthcare cost compared to those without this condition when matched by sex, age, and geographic region.
Studies done in Australia found that chronic health conditions such as LBP were a significant cause for early retirement and resultant income poverty.

Globally, LBP was the top cause of years lived with disability (YLDs) in 1990 and 2013, and it was among the top 10 causes of YLDs in every country that was part of the Global Burden of Disease Study in 2013. This trend has continued in more recent years; LBP is one of the five leading causes of YLDs in 2016 globally.

A survey of the patterns of prescription medicine use among patients with CLBP showed that 77% are on long-term meds (most commonly opioids) frequently in combination with other CNS-active agents. CLBP is also associated with an increased risk for comorbid substance use disorders.
Nonspecific CLBP is the main focus of this chapter. Specific etiologic conditions are discussed separately in other chapters.
Per the NIH Task Force, overall transition of acute LBP to chronic LBP is 32%.

Etiologic causes for development and persistence of CLBP is unknown in about 85% of episodes in primary care—these are labelled 'nonspecific' due to inability to reliably ascribe the clinical picture to specific disease processes (eg, inflammation, malignancy, infection) or anatomic pathology (eg, fracture, nerve root compression).
Nonspecific or idiopathic

Mechanical: muscular strain or sprain, degenerative processes of spine or hip, disc herniation, spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis and spondylolysis, congenital or acquired disease (kyphosis, scoliosis), fracture (vertebral compression or osteoporotic fracture), myofascial pain syndrome, sacroiliac dysfunction

Nonmechanical: neoplasia (primary spine malignancy, metastases), inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic spondylitis, Reiter's syndrome), infection (osteomyelitis, septic discitis, paraspinous abscess, epidural abscess, zoster)

Referred pain: vascular (abdominal aortic aneurysm), gastrointestinal (cholelithiasis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, peptic ulcer disease), pelvic (endometriosis, chronic prostatitis, pelvic inflammatory disease), renal (nephrolithiasis, pyelonephritis, perinephric abscess)
Other: fibromyalgia, sickle cell crisis, Paget's disease of bone, Scheuermann disease
Unclear for nonspecific CLBP, but muscular and ligamentous strain and sprain are common Multifactorial etiology is ubiquitous.
Development of muscular pathology (fatty infiltration, fibrosis, and possible atrophy) that leads to decrease function and rehabilitative potential have been implicated.
For myofascial pain syndrome, pain sensation in nociceptive receptors in muscle spindles result in tight bands which translate to trigger points on physical exam.

In degenerative disc disease, changes in the intervertebral disc with aging plus continuous use microtrauma result in inflammation. In addition, biomechanical, genetic, environmental, and psychosocial factors come into play leading to dysfunction and instability in the lumbar spine. Osteophyte formation and pain sensitization of spinal nerves and centralization follow, forming the pathway to chronicity.

Increased pain sensitization (initially peripheral, later becoming centralized) may be the mechanism by which transition of acute LBP to chronic LBP is facilitated through disruptions in the mesocorticolimbic (dopaminergic) reward circuits in the brain. These pathways also serve to regulate motivated behavioral responses to pain relief as well as the affective component of pain.
In older patients with CLBP there is increased involvement of the limbic area of the brain compared to younger cohorts.
In the presence of radiculopathy, there is dysfunction of a nerve root that causes pain, sensory impairment, weakness, and/or diminished deep tendon reflexes within a nerve root distribution.
In the presence of spinal stenosis, there is narrowing of the spinal canal that may cause bony constriction of the cauda equina and the emerging nerve roots.

list.listitem: Lumbar supports and insoles are not effective in preventing LBP. A

Training and advising employees on proper lifting techniques and use of assistive devices are not effective in preventing back pain or back pain-related disability (moderate quality evidence) as these interventions do not necessarily translate to behavioral changes. A
Workplace back pain prevention programs are ineffective in preventing back pain or reducing work absences or costs compared with usual care. B

For low income communities, based on the Global Spine Care Initiative, affordability and accessibility of interventions, along with self-care, patient education and nonpharmacologic treatment options should be prioritized in treatment planning. Conservative, noninvasive treatment modalities such as exercise, yoga, acupuncture, biofeedback cognitive behavioral therapies, progressive relaxation, massage, manual therapy, interdisciplinary rehabilitation are recommended. Recommended pharmacologic interventions may include NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and antidepressants.
Conduct a focused history and physical examination including assessment of psychosocial risk factors. C

Differential.Differential_Features: History of cancer, unexplained weight loss, and age older than 50 years
Urinary retention, fecal incontinence, motor deficits, and saddle anesthesia
Morning stiffness, pain improvement with exercise, and alternating buttock pain
Fever, intravenous drug use, and recent infection
History of osteoporosis, use of corticosteroids, and older age
Back pain with leg pain in an L4, L5, or S1 nerve root distribution, positive straight-leg-raise test
Radiating leg pain and older age

list.listitem: History: Inquire about the location, duration, frequency, severity, characteristics of pain, presence of radiation along with precipitating and alleviating factors, previous similar episode(s), prior evaluation and treatment modalities and their effectiveness, temporal changes in presentation to indicate symptom progression and effect of pain on daily function and activities. Assess risk of mechanical LBP with BMI, occupational hazards, and physical activity.

Physical Exam: valuable information come from vital signs and general appearance and behavior, mood and affect, judgement and thought processes. Start with inspection of the thoracolumbar spine and palpation over spinous processes. Do focused musculoskeletal and neurologic exam of the back and legs including ROM, tests of strength and sensation, and reflexes of lower extremities. Observe gait, station and transfers, and do specific functional/provocation tests for specific disorders (eg. Straight leg test/crossed straight leg test for lumbar disc herniation; Patrick’s (FABER) test and Gaenslen’s test for sacroiliac dysfunction).
Inquire about the presence of red flags () which may be indications of a more complicated clinical picture.
Inquire about history of comorbidities including psychiatric conditions and history of substance abuse, disability compensation, work status.
Certain history and physical exam findings point to specific diagnoses:

Suspect cancer in patients with onset over the age of 50 years, unexplained weight loss, previous history of cancer, no relief with bed rest, or no improvement after 1 month. Relief with bed rest is evidence against cancer as a diagnosis (LR− 0.01).

Suspect ankylosing spondylitis in patients whose pain gets them out of bed at night; in whom pain is not relieved by lying down but does improve with exercise; and who have morning stiffness, younger age at onset, alternating buttock pain, chest expansion less than 2.5 cm, and lateral spine flexion less than 10 cm. Anterior spine flexion greater than 5 cm and onset after the age of 40 years make the diagnosis less likely.

Suspect spinal stenosis in patients with no pain or symptom improvement when seated, wide-based gait (LR+ 14.3), abnormal Romberg test (LR+ 4.3), and neurologic deficits: weakness, sensory deficit, absent Achilles reflex (LR+ 2.1-2.8).

Suspect disc herniation in patients with sciatica, ipsilateral or especially crossed straight-leg raise or great toe extensor weakness. Absence of complaint of sciatica (pain radiating below the knee) makes the diagnosis very unlikely (LR- 0.06).

Older age, corticosteroid use, trauma, and presence of a contusion or abrasion may increase the likelihood of a vertebral fracture. A combination of these findings may increase the likelihood, but individually these findings have high false positive rates. The cost-effectiveness of screening using individual or a combination of these findings has not been evaluated.
A history of malignancy increases the probability of malignancy as a cause of low back pain to 7% in primary care and 33% in emergency department settings.
Suspect fibromyalgia in patients with multiple symmetric areas of pain and tenderness.
Although rare, consider spinal osteomyelitis or epidural abscess in patients with fever, risk factors for abscess, or spinal tenderness to percussion may be seen in spinal osteomyelitis.
Diagnostic imaging should not be routinely ordered for patients presenting with nonspecific CLBP because there is no evidence to suggest that it is associated with improved patient outcomes.

According to the 2021 American College of Radiology (ACR) Update, for patients with CLBP with no red flags, with or without radiculopathy, imaging is not deemed as appropriate. For patients with CLBP with or without radiculopathy who have persistent or progressive symptoms during or after optimal medical management and are candidates for intervention or surgery, MRI of the lumbar spine without IV contrast is usually appropriate as are other imaging tests if indicated.
Simple clinical factors (using a decision support tool) can help identify patients likely to benefit from radiographic evaluation.

The North American Spine Society, as part of the Choosing Wisely Campaign, recommends against using electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies (NCS) to look for an underlying cause of axial lumbar pain.
The need for further workup through laboratory testing and imaging should be guided by clinical suspicion based on history and PE findings:
If cancer is suspected, order ESR, hematocrit, and plain radiographs. If these are abnormal or there remains a high index of suspicion based on history, order MRI or CT imaging.
If ankylosing spondylitis is suspected, order plain radiography, CRP, and HLA-B27.
If spinal stenosis is suspected, order MRI and/or EMG/NCS if the patient is experiencing prolonged symptoms.
If disc herniation is suspected, particularly if a new or worsening neurologic deficit is present, consider MRI or CT.
Simple clinical factors can help identify patients likely to benefit from radiographic evaluation.
A clinical decision rule has been developed to guide return to work decisions, but has not been prospectively validated.
A validated risk score uses 3 items (number of episodes, severity of pain, and duration of pain) to predict likelihood of rapid recovery.
See algorithm in .
Guidelines from the VA/DoD recommend a holistic approach that is patient-centered. Shared decision-making that considers comorbidities and goals of treatment is encouraged.

Acetaminophen, anticonvulsants, gabapentinoids, muscle relaxants, benzodiazepines, B SSRIs, A and cannabinoids C are not recommended for long-term management of CLBP given their lack of clear efficacy. Anticonvulsants, gabapentinoids, and benzodiazepines are associated with higher risk for adverse events. B

Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) only have modest efficacy for CLBP and their use may be associated with increased risk for side effects. A
Opioids show no clear benefit in CLBP and are associated with adverse events and other harmful effects. B

Topical capsaicin cream (low quality evidence) B and topical Cayenne pepper A appear to be effective and may be considered as treatment options especially in patients at high risk for systemic side effects with oral medications, but careful monitoring of local reactions is recommended.

Exercise should be considered early in the course of treatment as it is effective, generally safe, and may have enduring effects. No single type of exercise is superior and manual therapies may be just as effective. A

The evidence is inconclusive for the effectiveness of osteopathic manipulative therapy (OMT) in CLBP; kinesiotaping and spinal manipulation show no clear benefit. Do not order therapeutic ultrasound and traction for CLBP as they are ineffective. B
Surgery may not offer substantial benefits over non-surgical treatment modalities for CLBP. B
Acupuncture may have limited effectiveness for CLBP in the short term. Massage may be modestly effective in the short term.B
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has modest efficacy for CLBP that may be sustained in the long term. Consider combination with physical therapy for enhanced effectiveness. A

Workplace intervention programs may help reduce absenteeism due to CLBP from musculoskeletal problems. A Physical conditioning as part of an integrated care management program may also have a modest effect on reducing absenteeism. B

Multidisciplinary biopsychosocial rehabilitation programs are effective but are cost- and labor-intensive and warrant careful patient selection. Patients with significant physical and psychosocial impacts from their condition would gain the most benefit. A

There is no evidence for the effectiveness of any specific nutritional, herbal, or homeopathic supplement or diet in CLBP. Caution on use is emphasized due to possible adverse effects and drug interactions given the variety of commercially available preparation and lack of industry regulation. C
There is no evidence for the effectiveness of acetaminophen in the treatment of CLBP.

In general, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) show modest efficacy for patient outcomes in CLBP (with certainty of evidence ranging from low to moderate) and may be associated with increased risk of adverse effects in the short and intermediate term. The following evidence support these generalizations:

NSAIDs have been shown to be better than placebo in decreasing pain intensity and disability although magnitude of effects were small and quality of evidence was low. There is no evidence of increased risk for side effects at intermediate term (>3 months and ≤12 months).

A 2020 Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) review showed similar results with small improvements in pain and function in the short term for CLBP from osteoarthritis. Risk for adverse events noted in the short term included increased risk for upper GI bleeding with non-selective NSAIDs, increased risk of coronary events with diclofenac, celecoxib and ibuprofen, but overall risk of CVD was not increased. In the intermediate term, increased risk for GI events with nonselective NSAIDs and liver dysfunction with diclofenac and naproxen were noted.
Based on low quality evidence, a 2023 Cochrane review found no difference in pain relief between antidepressants (all types) and placebo.

Moderate quality evidence show that serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) are somewhat effective in improving pain and disability scores in CLBP though effects were small and only limited to the short term. Duloxetine use was associated with more adverse events, mostly mild.

A meta-analysis of seven high quality trials found tricyclic and tetracylic antidepressants (TCAs) to be moderately effective for CLBP (benefit is independent of depression status) while SSRIs show no benefit. Low dose amitriptyline (25mg) showed effectiveness in reducing disability in the short term with minimal reported adverse events.
A Cochrane review in 2025 concluded that TCAs are likely ineffective for reducing pain intensity and only modestly improve disability in patients with CLBP; adverse events are uncertain.
Gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) and anticonvulsant topiramate have questionable effectivity in CLBP and are associated with higher rates of adverse events.
Benzodiazepines have questionable efficacy in CLBP and use is associated with a higher risk for adverse events.
There is no good evidence for the use of muscle relaxants in CLBP.

In general, in the short, intermediate, and long term, opioid analgesics do not show clear benefit. They have not been found to be superior and may be inferior to other analgesics such as antiinflammatories and antidepressants. Opioid use is associated with more adverse events, possibly dose-related, which include nausea, dizziness, somnolence, constipation, and vomiting. There is potential for opioid abuse and a 2022 systematic review noted a possible increase in all-cause mortality. Individual opioid drugs may have varying effects on pain and disability but they are generally small with low to moderate levels of certainty. These conclusions are based on the following:

In the short term (<3 months), while opioids show some efficacy in pain relief and improvement of function compared to placebo, they are no more effective than other analgesics such as antiinflammatories and antidepressants (very low to moderate quality evidence), and are associated with higher risk for adverse effects. A meta-analysis found very low certainty evidence that opioids provide benefit in the short term and that this effect disappeared after >4 weeks. Patients were also more likely to discontinue treatment due to higher rates of adverse events which included nausea, dizziness, somnolence, constipation and vomiting. Similar results were found by two recent systematic reviews.

In the long term (>12 months), opioids compared to nonopioid therapies were not superior in improving pain-related function and were inferior in relieving pain intensity. In one RCT, dropouts were significantly higher in the opioid group (19% vs 8%). A meta-analysis similarly found that opioids may not be superior to nonopioids for pain improvement, function and disability in the long term and may be associated with more adverse events including opioid abuse, noting a possible increase in all-cause mortality. Another systematic review concluded that evidence on intermediate- and long-term benefits of opioid use for CLBP remain very limited and noted that there is evidence for dose-dependent increased risk for serious harms with opioid use.
A Cochrane review concluded that opioids could have a small effect on pain and disability based on very low to high certainty evidence.

The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons and the North American Spine Society, as part of the Choosing Wisely Campaign, recommend against the routine use of opioids for CLBP treatment. The CDC Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Chronic Pain recommends nonopioid therapy as the preferred treatment. All three advocate for thorough evaluation, consideration of alternative treatments and medications, performing concurrent medication review and discussion of opioid therapy risks and potential interactions. If deemed appropriate in extraordinary circumstances, the lowest effective opioid dose for a limited time should be used.
One RCT found no difference between flurbiprofen tape (a topical NSAID) and placebo in relieving CLBP.
3 RCTs with low quality evidence found capsaicin cream to be effective in reducing pain compared to placebo (NNT 6) but reports of adverse reaction of heat sensation was more common (NNTH 3).

Overall, surgery may not offer substantial benefits over non-surgical treatment modalities for CLBP. For patients who undergo surgery, adding fusion to decompression surgery may not result in improved patient outcomes. Epidural steroid injections, radiofrequency (RF) facet joint denervation, and spinal cord stimulation are likely not beneficial for CLBP.

Multiple RCTs found no difference between surgical intervention (spinal fusion or laminectomy) and non-operative treatment (involving exercise rehabilitation and CBT program) even at long term follow-up (8-15 years). One recent systematic review echoed this finding, noting that on average only 14% of all studies found surgery beneficial. Two older studies found some benefit for surgery but both had high levels of nonadherence in the participants and other limitations.

For patients who undergo surgery, adding fusion to decompression surgery does not seem to offer any added improvement in patient outcomes, although reoperation ws noted to be slightly higher in the decompression-only group.

There is insufficient evidence to support the use of injection therapy (eg, intra-articular injections, periarticular injections, and nerve blocks) in CLBP. A systematic review, based on very low quality evidence, found corticosteroid injections to be ineffective for CLBP.
Steroid disc injection for patients with evidence of disc inflammation on MRI produced a short-term benefit that disappeared after 1 year.

The North American Spine Society, as part of the Choosing Wisely Campaign, recommends that elective cases of spinal injections be performed with imaging guidance (ie, fluoroscopy or CT with contrast enhancement) to ensure that both diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic efficacy are maximized.

RF facet joint denervation (RFD) has not been shown to be effective in improving pain or disability in CLBP. A combined report from 3 RCTs involving 681 patients with CLBP due to facet joint, sacroiliac joint (or a combination), or intervertebral disc showed no benefit for adding RFD to a standardized exercise program.

A 2023 systematic review of 13 RCTs concluded that SCS should not be recommended as treatment for CLBP outside of clinical trials. Lack of sustained benefits and high risk of bias in the studies, coupled with cost and risk of serious adverse events with the procedure, limit its clinical applicability. Similar results were reported by a 2021 systematic review of 15 RCTs.
Evidence is inconclusive for prolotherapy and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS).
Currently, no rigorous studies have been done to evaluate the efficacy of cannabinoids for CLBP.

Some topical medicines (capsaicin cream, Cayenne) show some efficacy and may be considered as treatment options especially in patients with considerably higher risk for systemic side effects with oral medicines, but careful monitoring of local reactions should be done. There is no evidence yet of safety or efficacy of these substances for long term use.

A 2014 Cochrane review found low-quality evidence that some herbal medicines may provide more relief of nonspecific LBP than placebo. However, based on the 2022 Veterans Affair/Department of Defense guidelines, there is no evidence for the effectiveness of any specific nutritional, herbal, or homeopathic supplement or diet in CLBP. Caution on use is emphasized due to possible adverse effects and drug interactions given the variety of commercially available preparation and lack of industry regulation.
A meta-analysis of poor-quality trials found that devil's claw, white willow bark, and topical capsaicin may provide modest analgesia in acute episodes of CLBP.
Placebo tablets produce short-term improvements in CLBP compared to usual care, even when patients are told that they are taking placebo.
An RCT of 250 adults with degenerative lumbar osteoarthritis found that glucosamine was not more effective than placebo for reducing CLBP or improving quality of life.

A Cochrane review concluded that acupuncture may have limited efficacy for CLBP in the short term. No acupuncture technique was shown to be superior and these interventions are generally considered to be safe.

A trial randomized 216 participants with unilateral sciatica from herniated disk for more than 3 months, with moderate to severe leg pain to acupuncture or sham acupuncture (needles inserted but at the wrong place). Scores on the Oswestry Disability Index decreased an average 13 points in the treatment group versus 5 points in the control group (a difference of 7 or greater is clinically relevant). Treatment benefit began in the second week of treatment and was still significant at 52 weeks.
One RCT (N=90) found no benefit of dry cupping over sham cupping in patients with nonspecific CLBP.
One RCT found that viniyoga, which combines yoga poses, breathing and meditation, decreased functional disability more effectively than exercise or self-care.

Multiple Cochrane and systematic reviews found moderate certainty evidence for the effectiveness of exercise in improving pain and disability scores in patients with CLBP compared to no treatment, usual care, or placebo. Exercise was also shown to be more effective than electrotherapy, education, or advice only, but no difference was found between exercise and treatments involving manual physical therapies. Quality of life was also noted to improve, and exercise was considered to be generally safe.

One review emphasized that exercise was the only intervention among commonly used nonpharmacologic treatments that showed sustained benefits in the long term (up to 48weeks). An AHRQ review found no difference when exercise was compared to low level laser therapy, spinal manipulation, massage, and yoga but quality of evidence was low.
One small RCT found no difference between remote and in-person exercise instruction in improving pain and disability scores for up to 3 months after intervention.

Multiple systematic reviews assessed different forms of exercise for CLBP. Pilates, yoga, and motor control exercise (MCE) all showed some effectiveness in pain and function over non-exercise or minimal intervention with low to moderate quality evidence. Risk of adverse events was low and no one exercise is more effective than the others.

MCE focusing on training deep trunk muscles to promote spinal control and coordination with biofeedback, while effective compared to minimal intervention, is no different from manual therapies (moderate to high quality evidence).

Walking or cycling showed high-certainty evidence of a small effect over minimal or no treatment, but may be less effective than alternative interventions (ranging from meds to passive and active physical modalities including other exercise) for recurrent or CLBP.

An RCT in younger adults (average age 31 years) found that aquatherapy was more effective than physiotherapy modalities (nerve stimulation and infrared ray thermal therapy) at improving pain and disability scores at 3, 6, and 12 months.
Exercise treatment starting 4 to 6 weeks after lumbar disc surgery seem to speed reduction in pain and disability.

There is moderate quality evidence to support the effectiveness of multidisciplinary biopsychosocial rehab programs in improving pain and function. Less intensive programs are not as effective. However, the cost and labor-intensiveness of such programs warrant careful patient selection. Those determined to have significant physical and psychosocial impacts from their condition appear to gain the most from this intervention.
Evidence of effectiveness is uncertain for 'Back Schools' which are therapeutic programs that combine education and exercise.

In one study, intensive rehabilitation (education + exercise) reduced disability but was slightly less effective than spinal fusion surgery. Complications occurred in 11% of patients treated with surgery; there were no complications in the rehabilitation group.
Massage may be modestly effective for CLBP in the short term.

Based on low to very low certainty evidence, spinal manipulative therapy (SMT), compared to sham SMT/placebo or to no treatment, may be effective in improving pain and functional status among patients with CLBP. However, it is no more effective than other conservative or traditional therapies (eg, exercise, physical therapy, standard medical care).
The evidence is inconclusive for the effectiveness of osteopathic manipulative therapy (OMT) for CLBP.
A meta-analysis found low quality evidence for benefit with kinesiotaping in pain and disability improvement.
A Cochrane review found low to moderate certainty evidence that traction (both manual and mechanical) is not effective for CLBP.
Therapeutic ultrasound for CLBP is not supported by current evidence.
A 2020 AHRQ systematic review found moderate quality evidence that psychological therapies were associated with small improvements in pain and function in the short, intermediate, and long-term.

A Cochrane review found cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to be moderately effective. Another meta-analysis found low to high quality evidence that psychological interventions (eg, behavior therapy, CBT, pain education) are most effective when combined with physical therapy (mainly structured exercise) and result in clinical improvement for up to 6 to 12 months.

Mindfulness based stress reduction (MBSR) is effective in improving pain, disability and quality of life, but the data is conflicting as to duration. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that the effects were only short term, while one RCT found effects persisted up to 52 weeks.
2 RCTs found that cognitive functional therapy (CFT) may be more effective than manual therapy plus exercise at reducing disability but not pain.
Alexander technique to reduce muscle tension through self-awareness of body posture and movement may reduce pain and disability and appears be cost-effective compared to usual care in one RCT.

Intensive tele-health delivered cognitive therapy, behavioral activation, and mindfulness meditation all appear beneficial for CLBP, based on a single-blinded RCT evaluating 302 patients with low back pain for at least 3 months. Given the established effectiveness of these interventions, the study authors determined it was unethical to have a sham therapy or usual care control group. All of the interventions showed improvement in pain interference (medium to large effect), pain intensity and sleep disturbance (small to medium effect).

Bed rest is not recommended for CLBP. Continued physical activity should be encouraged as data from experimental studies found evidence that continuous mechanical loading of the spine promotes general intervertebral disc health through increased diffusion of nutrients and induction of regenerative processes.
There are no good studies for the use of superficial heat or cold therapy in CLBP.
Evidence of effectiveness is uncertain for intensive patient education

For workers on disability related to back pain, there is moderate quality evidence that workplace intervention programs (ie, changes to the workplace/equipment, work design/organization, working conditions/environment, and worker/supervisor involvement), when compared to usual care or clinical interventions, reduce duration of sickness absence days and improve pain and functional status for those with exclusive musculoskeletal disorders but not for those with mental health problems or cancer.

Furthermore, an integrated care management program that includes physical/work conditioning or hardening and functional restoration plus back pain education, behavioral operant conditioning approach, pain management, workplace involvement and case management, when compared to usual care, results in reduced sickness absence days for up to a year, though quality of evidence is low and the most effective part of the integrated care management is unclear.
Alternative care models do not appear to yield clinically meaningful improvement in patient outcomes compared to usual care.

Because pharmacologic interventions only provide modest evidence of efficacy in the short term and may have adverse effects, long term use of medications is not advised. These interventions should be used in the shortest possible time that gives the maximal benefit. Nonpharmacologic interventions should be employed primarily, with pharmacologic therapies reserved for acute flares of CLBP.
Consider referring to physical therapy and behavioral interventions early.
Consider surgical consultation if there is a clear indication, such as progressive or severe neurologic deficits or spinal cord compression.

Meaningful improvement of CLBP may be expected in the first 6 weeks of diagnosis but slows down within a year. Placebo effect may contribute initially, but low to moderate pain and disability usually persist after a year for a significant subset of patients. B
Recurrences are common and may be associated with certain medical, behavioral, and social factors. B Good continuity of care and clear clinical indications for workup and referral are important. C
Patients’ recovery expectations are associated with clinical recovery outcomes B and future work participation outcomes. A
A non-validated clinical decision rule may help determine the likelihood of successfully returning to work and directing high-risk patients into more intensive therapy. B
An inception cohort study found that for recent onset CLBP, 35% will recover by 9 months and 41% recover by 1 year.

In patients with persistent LBP, marked improvement in pain and disability may be expected in the first 6 weeks but slows down subsequently. Moderate levels of pain and disability could be expected at one year.

Recurrences are common. In one prospective inception cohort study, 69% of participants had a recurrence of LBP within 12 months of previous recovery. Predictive factors include frequent exposure to awkward postures, sitting >5 hours per day, and >2 previous LBP episodes.

A systematic review found that the mean reduction on a 100 point standardized pain scale was 8 points in the first 6 weeks, 5 points in weeks 6 to 26, and 3 points from weeks 26 to 52. Over one year the mean pain score decreased from 56 to 40 points.
An older systematic review did not find good estimates of the risk of or prognostic factors for LBP recurrence.

One inception cohort study in Australia with 973 participants found less than 1/3 had completely recovered in 12 months. A similar study of 406 participants with CLBP found that greater than 1/3 of patients recover within a year. Factors associated with delayed recovery included high pain intensity at onset of chronicity, low educational levels, greater perceived risk of persistent pain and being born outside the country. A similar but older study with more participants found less than 1/3 had completely recovered after 12 months.

A Cochrane review found prognostic value for individual patient’s recovery expectations. These are probably strongly associated with future work participation outcomes (moderate-quality evidence) and clinical recovery outcomes (low-quality evidence).
Regarding the placebo effect, one RCT found short-term improvements in pain intensity and disability (also depression) even when patients know they are taking placebo.

A prospective observational cohort study found that on long term follow up, patients with lumbar spinal stenosis who received nonsurgical treatment had similar pain relief, symptom improvement and satisfaction compared to their surgically-treated cohorts.

A clinical decision rule may help determine the likelihood of successfully returning to work and directing high-risk patients into more intensive therapy. However, it has not been prospectively validated.

Since CLBP may be recurrent and marked by episodes of acute exacerbation, good continuity care with a provider who knows individual patients’ comorbidities is recommended so shared decision-making and treatment goals are discussed and revisited.
There should be clear clinical indications for ordering diagnostic workup and referral to subspecialities.
CLBP may be recurrent requiring periodic visits to the doctor and pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions (physical therapy, behavioral therapies).
Avoid bed rest and remain physically active as much as possible.
A positive prognostic outlook may be helpful as a patient's expectation for recovery may affect course of clinical recovery and future work participation.
Approach interpreting online and social media information on CLBP with caution considering the for-profit nature of these companies and the poor-quality of the information.

Age older than 55 years may be a red flag for LBP, and LBP should be investigated more thoroughly at an earlier stage in the disease course due to higher risk for more pathologic processes (eg, neoplasm, compression fracture, etc).

Staying physically active is recommended. Experimental studies found evidence that in degenerative disc conditions, continuous mechanical loading of the spine promotes general intervertebral disc health through increased diffusion of nutrients and induction of regenerative processes.
One RCT involving geriatric patients found the concomitant use of opioids lowers the pain response to venlafaxine (in a opioid dose-dependent manner) compared to those only taking the SNRI.

The 'geriatric syndrome' approach to CLBP promotes care through Aging Back Clinics (ABCs), a comprehensive, patient-centered program specifically tailored for patients ≥60 years old with CLBP but no red flags. Preliminary data comparing ABCs to usual care found efficacy in pain relief, quality of life, and health care utilization measures.

A cohort study of community-dwelling older adults with CLBP found that favorable prognosis is consistent with certain factors: fewer depressive symptoms and comorbidities, higher physical activity levels, lower LBP intensities, less pain-related fear and catastrophizing.
Unless there are red flags, delay diagnostic testing and focus on nonpharmacologic interventions.
Reserve radiologic studies for patients with red flags due to the risks of exposure to the fetus. The second trimester is the ideal time to conduct such studies to minimize risk.
The changes in body habitus and hormonal changes of pregnancy contribute to CLBP that usually resolves after delivery.

cell.label: Patient with low back pain (LBP) >3 months. Perform focused history and physical including duration, risk factors, and presence and severity of symptoms.
Could LBP be due to serious cause (eg, cancer, ankylosing spondylitis, vertebral infection, cauda equine, or vertebral compression fracture)?
Diagnostic studies are not recommended. Discuss pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic (ie, physical therapy, massage, and spinal manipulation) treatment options.
Cauda equine syndrome suspected (eg, bowel/bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, and progressive deficit)?
Vertebral infection suspected (eg, fever, recent instrumentation, and elevated WBC)?
Herniated disk or spinal stenosis suspected?
Cancer suspected (eg, weight loss, elevated sedimentation rate, history of malignancy, and other symptoms?)
Vertebral compression fracture suspected (eg, over the age of 50 years, history of osteopenia or osteoporosis, trauma)?
Ankylosing spondylitis suspected (eg, insidious onset before the age of 40 years, associated with morning stiffness, and improvement with exercise)?
Anterior-posterior pelvis plain radiography, consider HLA-B27 testing.

tr.td: History of spinal procedure in the past 12months
History of or current IV drug use or substance abuse
History of cancer/strong suspicion for current cancer
Minor fall or heavy lifting in potentially osteoporotic or elderly patient
Unrelenting night pain or pain at rest
Acute onset of overflow incontinence or urinary retention
Fecal incontinence or loss of anal sphincter tone
Progressive motor or sensory deficit in legs
Progressive or bilateral weakness of lower limbs
